---
title: Brewing black tea
lang: en
free: true
---

Black tea rewards full heat and a confident steep. The leaves are fully oxidized, which means they can stand up to near-boiling water without turning harsh the way more delicate teas do.

## Water temperature

Pour water as close to 100°C as you can manage. Fully oxidized leaves need that heat to release their depth — the dark, malty, sometimes fruity notes that define a good cup. Letting the water cool first only flattens the result.

## Steeping

Two to four minutes is the usual window, depending on how strong you like it. Check at two minutes, taste, and pull the leaves or bag when the flavour suits you. Leaving it longer extracts more tannin and produces the familiar dry, astringent finish that some enjoy and others find unpleasant.

Milk softens the tannins and is a reasonable addition with strong, brisk teas like Assam. With single-origin Darjeeling or Ceylon, try it plain first so the floral notes are not masked. One steep is usually all you get from a good quality bag; loose leaf can take a second pour if the first steep was short.
